1.pericope_label: Now when Festus was come into the province, after three days he ascended from Caesarea to Jerusalem. Then the high priest and the chief of the Jews informed him against Paul, and besought him, and desired favour against him, that he would send for him to Jerusalem, laying wait in the way to kill him. But Festus answered, that Paul should be kept at Caesarea, and that he himself would depart shortly thither. Let them therefore, said he, which among you are able, go down with me, and accuse this man, if there be any wickedness in him

schools.summary: Set the geography and the persons. Into the province means the province of Judea, for Judea at that time was a Roman province. He ascended was the usual language which described a journey to Jerusalem, as the English speak of going up to London, because it is the capital. The governors of Judea at this time usually resided at Caesarea; but as Jerusalem had been the former capital, as it was still the seat of the religious solemnities, as the council held its meetings there, and as the great, the rich, the learned and the priests resided there, a full knowledge of the state of the province could be obtained only there, so Festus early went up to make himself acquainted with the affairs of the nation. The high priest at this time was Ismael the son of Fabi, promoted to that office by Agrippa, according to the historian; it is probable, however, that the person here intended was Ananias, who had been high priest and would retain the name. Some manuscripts read high priests in the plural. They informed him of the accusation and doubtless endeavoured to prejudice his mind, and thus showed their unrelenting disposition: it might have been supposed that after two years this unjust prosecution would be abandoned and forgotten, but malice does not thus forget its object, and the spirit of persecution is not thus satisfied. Festus was a stranger to Paul, and would wish to conciliate the favour of the nation on entering on the duties of his office, so a strong representation by the chief men would be likely to prejudice him. They desired the favour of Festus that they might accomplish their wicked purpose, probably under a pretence that Paul might be tried by the council; their real motive is immediately stated, for they would lie in wait, or employ a band of assassins, to take his life on the journey. Had this request been granted, Paul would altogether probably have been killed; but God had promised that he should bear witness at Rome, and his providence was remarkable in thus influencing the mind of the Roman governor. What induced Festus to refuse is not known, but it is probable that he was apprized that Paul was a Roman citizen, and that his case could not come before the Jewish council but must be heard by himself; and as Caesarea was the residence of the governor and the place of holding the courts, there was no sufficient reason for a removal. He granted them all that they could reasonably ask: let them enjoy all the advantages of a just trial, and exhibit their accusations with all the learning and talent in their power. Elsewhere weigh the words and the manuscripts. He ascended is better rendered, he went up. Some of the best manuscripts give the plural, the chief priests. It is clear that they hoped to take advantage of the newness of Festus to his office: he was likely enough, they thought, to accept their statements and to yield to the pressure of those who had shown themselves powerful enough to bring about his predecessor’s recall. And they have not forgotten their old tactics: once again priests and scribes are ready to avail themselves of the weapon of the assassin. Possibly Festus had heard from Felix or from the tribune of the former plot, and took care to be on his guard against this, so that the conspirators were again baffled. Which among you are able: the adjective is probably used in the sense of powerful or chief, rather than as referring to their being able to accuse the man of whom they had complained. What Festus demanded was that the charges should be supported by the leaders and representatives of the people, and not by a hired rhetorician. If there be any wickedness in him: the better manuscripts give simply, if there be anything, that is, anything worth inquiring into. Elsewhere keep to the grammar. Having come into the province is a second aorist active participle of a verb meaning to set foot upon: literally, having set foot upon his province. The word for province is a late word, in the New Testament only here and at the tribune’s question earlier; Judea was not strictly a province, but a department of the province of Syria, which was under a legate of Caesar while Judea was under a procurator. After three days means on the third day, with a day of rest in between — precisely the language used of the resurrection of Jesus, after three days meaning on the third day, by common usage then and now. The principal men are the first men, the leading men of the city, besides the chief priests; there was another high priest now, Ishmael in place of Ananias. Of the renewal of the charge it has been said that this renewal after two years, on the very first opportunity, is a measure not only of their unsleeping hatred, but of the importance which they attached to Paul’s influence. Besought is imperfect active: they kept on beseeching as a special favour. Asking favour against him is middle voice, a favour to themselves, and the preposition is down against him. Laying wait is an old idiom for laying a plot or ambush, used only twice in the New Testament; two years before, the council had agreed to the plot of the forty conspirators, and now they propose one on their own initiative. On the way means down along the way, and plenty of opportunity would occur between Caesarea and Jerusalem for ambush and surprise attacks. Festus was clearly suspicious and was wholly within his rights to insist that they make their charges in Caesarea where he held court; shortly means in quickness, and he did go down in eight or ten days. Them therefore which are of power among you means the mighty ones, the men of power and authority, the first men, the council in other words; note the change here from indirect discourse to direct. Go down with me is a double compound participle, and it was a fair proposal. If there is anything amiss in the man is a condition of the first class, assuming that there is, to be courteous to them, but not committing himself on the merits of the case; the word rendered amiss is an old word, specially common in one philosopher, meaning out of place.

Read the danger and the providence together. The second action is described in this place, wherein Paul hath as hard a combat, and is in no less danger than in the first. Seeing he was left in bonds, Festus might suspect that the cause was doubtful, and so gather an unjust prejudice. But there was another thing which was cause of great danger: we know that new rulers, because they will win the favour of those who are in the provinces, use to grant them many things at their first coming, so that it was to be thought that the death of Paul should be to Festus a fine means to win favour with all. Therefore the faith of the holy man is assailed afresh with a new trial, as if the promise had been vain whereto he had hitherto trusted; but the grace of God doth so much the more plainly show itself in delivering him, because, contrary to all hope, he is delivered out of the jaws of death. The Jews prevent the governor with their false accusations, yet they do not as yet seek to have him punished, but only desire that he may not be brought into any foreign court to plead his cause; they desire that ambitiously as a great benefit, which was to look to equal. How is it then that they do not obtain, save only because God doth hold the mind of Festus, so that he doth stoutly deny that which he was afterward ready to grant? And as the Lord did then hold his mind bound with the secret bridle of his providence, so when he granted him freedom of will he bound his hands, that he could not execute that which he would. Let this confidence support us in dangers. On the last clause: it is in the Greek word for word, those who are mighty or able, yet he meaneth those who can conveniently. We may easily conjecture that they did object the trouble and charges, and besought the governor that he would not make weary with a superfluous journey so many of their chief men, and also certain which were very aged, but would rather command Paul to be brought by a few guards. Therefore, lest they complain that he is burdensome unto them, he unloadeth them of this necessity, and giveth them leave to choose out from among themselves such as they will. In the mean season he doth sufficiently declare that he doth not believe their false reports, and professeth that he will be an upright judge, and will do nothing but according to the truth of the matter. The next sentence also is diversely read among the Greeks: some manuscripts have but eight or ten days, and if this reading like us the sense shall be that the governor came shortly after to Caesarea, lest the Jews should be importunate upon him under colour of his long tarriance; the other reading shall have another meaning, that though he stayed long enough at Jerusalem to hear the matter, yet did he not hearken to their requests, whence we may gather a probable conjecture that he already knew of their laying await. Elsewhere fill in the persons and the sense. Festus was come into the province of Judea, over which he was made governor by Nero, in the room of Felix; he now being landed at Caesarea might be said to have entered upon the government of it. The high priest means, as several copies and versions read, the chief priests, the whole college of the priests. They desired favour against him: they asked what would be a favour to them and a prejudice to him; or of him, that is, of Festus, they asked a favour of him and desired it as such, as what would be gratefully accepted and acknowledged by them. But Festus answered that Paul was kept at Caesarea, in proper custody, under the care of a centurion, and should continue there, nor was there any reason why he should be removed, especially since he should return thither speedily. Let them therefore which among you are able: who are at leisure, can spare time, and to whom it will be convenient without interrupting other business to take such a journey; and who are able to bear the expense of it without hurting their families, and whose health and age will admit of it; and above all, who are masters of this affair, and are capable of forming charges and of supporting them with proper proofs and evidences.

Draw out the malice and then the providence. We commonly say, new lords, new laws, new customs; but here was a new governor, and yet Paul had the same treatment from him that he had from the former, and no better. Festus, like Felix, is not so just to him as he should have been, for he does not release him; and yet not so unjust to him as the Jews would have had him to be, for he will not condemn him to die, nor expose him to their rage. See first how speedy they were: as soon as ever he had come into the province he went up to Jerusalem, and presently the priests were upon him to proceed against Paul. He stayed three days at Caesarea, where Paul was a prisoner, and we do not find that in that time Paul made any application to him to release him, though no doubt he could have made good friends; but as soon as ever he comes up to Jerusalem the priests are in all haste to make an interest with him against Paul. See how restless a thing malice is: Paul more patiently bears the lengthening out of his imprisonment than his enemies do the delay of his prosecution even to the death. See next how spiteful they were: they informed the governor against Paul before he was brought upon a fair trial, that so they might prejudge the cause with the governor, and make him a party who was to be the judge. But this artifice they could not confide in, for the governor would be sure to hear him himself; and therefore they form another project much more base, and that is to assassinate Paul before he came upon his trial. These inhuman methods, which all the world profess at least to abhor, have these persecutors recourse to, to gratify their malice against the gospel of Christ, and this too under colour of zeal for Moses. See next how specious the pretence was: now that the governor was himself at Jerusalem they desired he would send for Paul thither and try him there, which would save the prosecutors a great deal of labour, and looked most reasonable, because he was charged with having profaned the temple at Jerusalem, and it is usual for criminals to be tried in the court where the fact was committed. But that which they designed was to way-lay him as he was brought up, and to murder him upon the road, supposing that he would not be brought up under so strong a guard as he was sent down with, or that the officers might be bribed. It is said they desired favour against Paul. The business of prosecutors is to demand justice against one that they suppose to be a criminal, and if he be not proved so it is as much justice to acquit him as it is to condemn him if he be; but to desire favour against a prisoner, and from the judge too, who ought to be of counsel for him, is a very impudent thing. The favour ought to be for the prisoner, to favour his life, but here they desire it against him. Then see how the governor manages the prosecutors. He will not do them the kindness to send for Paul to Jerusalem. It does not appear that he had any suspicion, much less any certain information, of their bloody design; but perhaps he was not willing to oblige the high priest and his party, or he would maintain the honour of his court at Caesarea, or he was not willing to be at the trouble or charge of bringing Paul up. Whatever was his reason, God made use of it as a means of preserving Paul out of the hands of his enemies. Though God does not, as before, bring the plot to light, yet he finds another way, as effectual, to bring it to nought, by inclining the heart of the governor, for some other reasons, not to remove Paul to Jerusalem. God is not tied to one method in working out salvation for his people: he can suffer the designs against them to be concealed, and yet not suffer them to be accomplished, and can make even the carnal policies of great men to serve his gracious purposes. Yet he will do them the justice to hear what they have to say, if they will go down to Caesarea: let those among you who are able, able in body and purse for such a journey, or able in mind and tongue to manage the prosecution, go down with me and accuse this man. Festus will not take it for granted that there is wickedness in him till it is proved upon him, and he has been heard in his own defence; but if he be guilty, it lies upon them to prove him so.

Give the story, then the surprise, then the demand. Porcius Festus being appointed governor of Judea instead of Felix, the Jews beseech him to have Paul brought up to Jerusalem that he might be tried there, they lying in wait to kill him on the way; Festus refuses, and desires those who could prove any thing against him to go with him to Caesarea. The high priest informed him against Paul: they supposed that as Felix, to please them, on the resignation of his government had left Paul bound, so Festus, on the assumption of it, would to please them deliver him into their hand; but as they wished this to be done under the colour of justice, they exhibited a number of charges against Paul, which they hoped would appear to Festus a sufficient reason why a new trial should be granted, and he be sent to Jerusalem to take this trial. Their motive is mentioned in the succeeding verse. It is truly astonishing that Festus should refuse this favour to the heads of the Jewish nation, which to those who were not in the secret must appear so very reasonable, and especially as, on his coming to the government, it might be considered an act that was likely to make him popular, and he could have no interest in denying their request. But God had told Paul that he should testify of him at Rome, and he disposed the heart of Festus to act as he did, and thus disappointed the malice of the Jews and fulfilled his own gracious design. So had the providence of God disposed matters that Festus was obliged to return speedily to Caesarea, and thus had not time to preside in such a trial at Jerusalem; and this reason must appear sufficient to the Jews, especially as he gave them all liberty to come and appear against him. Let them which among you are able means those who have authority, for so is the word often used by good Greek authors and by the historian. Festus seems to have said: I have heard clamours from the multitude relative to this man, but on such clamours no accusation should be founded; yourselves have only the voice of the multitude as the foundation of the request which you now make. I cannot take up accusations which may affect the life of a Roman citizen on such pretences. Are there any respectable men among you, men in office and authority, whose character is a pledge for the truth of their depositions, who can prove any thing against him? If so, let these come down to Caesarea, and the cause shall be tried before me, and thus we shall know whether he be a malefactor or not. Elsewhere keep it brief and turn it to providence. The high priest and the chief of the Jews appeared against Paul: in so long a time their rage was not cooled; so much louder a call had Paul to the Gentiles. But Festus answered: so Festus’s care to preserve the imperial privileges was the means of preserving Paul’s life. By what invisible springs does God govern the world! With what silence, and yet with what wisdom and energy! Let those of you who are able, who are best able to undertake the journey and to manage the cause; if there be any wickedness in him — so he does not pass sentence before he hears the cause.

debates: Whether the high priest named here is Ismael or Ananias, and whether the text reads singular or plural.
Why Festus refused to move the trial to Jerusalem — law, jurisdiction, convenience, or providence.
Whether those who are able means those with the means to travel or those with authority to accuse.
Whether Festus already knew of the plot against Paul.
outliers: Henry observes that the favour asked ought to have been for the prisoner, not against him.
Robertson notes that after three days here matches the idiom used of the resurrection.
Clarke composes a speech for Festus refusing to act on the clamour of a multitude.
Calvin reports a textual variant on how long Festus stayed at Jerusalem.
Ellicott suspects Festus had been warned of the earlier conspiracy.

6.pericope_label: And when he had tarried among them more than ten days, he went down unto Caesarea; and the next day sitting on the judgment seat commanded Paul to be brought. And when he was come, the Jews which came down from Jerusalem stood round about, and laid many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove. While he answered for himself, Neither against the law of the Jews, neither against the temple, nor yet against Caesar, have I offended any thing at all. But Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure, answered Paul, and said, Wilt thou go up to Jerusalem, and there be judged of these things before me?

schools.summary: Settle the reading, then the procedure. On more than ten days, see the margin: one version reads eight or ten, another not more than eight or ten, and a leading editor supposes this to be the true reading and has admitted it into the text. Sitting in the judgment seat means on the tribunal, holding a court for the trial of Paul; and he commanded Paul to be brought up for trial, who had been secured but placed in the care of a soldier commanded to let him have all the freedom consistent with his security. Grievous complaints are heavy accusations, doubtless the same with which they had charged him before Felix; and as the accusations against him were the same now as then, he made to them the same reply. On the governor’s proposal: he was desirous of securing their favour, as he had just entered on his administration, and in this he evinced rather a desire of popularity than an inclination to do justice, for had he been disposed to do right at once he would have immediately discharged Paul. Festus perceived that the case was one that did not come fairly within the jurisdiction of a Roman magistrate, but pertained solely to the customs and questions among the Jews, and he therefore proposed that it should be tried before him at Jerusalem. It is remarkable, however, that he had such a sense of justice and law as not to suffer the case to go out of his own hands: he proposed still to hear the cause, but asked Paul whether he was willing that it should be tried at Jerusalem. As the question was one on which Paul was at liberty to take his own course, and as he had no reason to expect that going to Jerusalem would facilitate the cause of justice, it is not remarkable that he declined the offer. Elsewhere reconstruct the indictment. Many and grievous complaints were, we may well believe, of the same nature as those on which the hired advocate had harangued; and the line of Paul’s defence indicates the three counts of the indictment. He had broken, it was alleged, the law of Israel, which Rome recognised as the religion of the province, and was therefore subject to the spiritual jurisdiction of the council; he had profaned the Temple; he was a disturber of the peace of the empire, and taught that there was another king than Nero. On the proposal: the invitation was in itself plausible enough. It practically admitted that there was no evidence on the last head of the accusation of which the governor, as procurator, need take cognizance. It offered the prisoner a trial before his own national tribunal, with the presence of the procurator as a check upon violence and injustice; and it is manifest from Paul’s answer that this was practically what Festus meant, for the proposed trial would, he says, not be before Caesar’s judgment seat, and he for his part preferred the secular to the ecclesiastical tribunal. Elsewhere keep to the grammar and the scene. On the morrow: Festus lost no time, for the chief men had come down with him. Sat on the judgment seat is an ingressive aorist participle, a legal formality to give weight to the decision, and the same phrase is repeated later in the chapter. Which had come down is a perfect active participle: they had come down on purpose at the invitation of Festus and were now ready. Stood round about him is a second aorist active of an old verb, they took their stand around him; they have no lawyer this time, but they mass their forces so as to impress Festus. Bringing against him means bearing down on. The word for charges is found in a papyrus in the sense of blame; but the charges were no heavier than those made before, as Paul’s reply proves. Which they could not prove is imperfect active of a verb meaning to have strength or power: repetition and reiteration and vehemence took the place of proof. While Paul said in his defence is a genitive absolute with a present middle participle. Have I sinned at all is a constative aorist, and Paul sums up the charges under the three items of the law of the Jews, the temple, and the Roman state. This last was the one that would interest Festus and, if proved, would render Paul guilty of treason. Nero was Emperor from the year fifty-four, the last of the emperors with any hereditary claim to the name Caesar; in this book only Caesar and Augustus are employed for the Emperor, not King. Paul’s denial is complete and no proof had been presented. Desiring to gain favour with the Jews is precisely the expression used of Felix earlier: Festus, like Felix, falls a victim to fear of the Jews. He now makes the very proposal to Paul that the rulers had made to him in Jerusalem, adding the words before me as if to insure Paul of justice. If Festus was unwilling to give Paul justice in Caesarea where his regular court held forth, what assurance was there that he would give it to him at Jerusalem in the atmosphere of intense hostility? Only two years ago the mob, the council and the forty conspirators had tried to take his life there. Festus had no more courage to do right than Felix, however plausible his language might sound; in reality he probably intended to turn Paul over to the council in order to please the Jews. It was not a mere change of venue that Paul sensed, but the utter unwillingness of Festus to do his duty by him.

Note the reading, then the slander, then the injustice. The Alexandrian copy and several others, with one Latin version, read no more than eight or ten days; the Syriac and Ethiopic leave out the phrase no more and read, when he had stayed there, that is, at Jerusalem. The historian, not being certain to a day, expresses himself in this manner. While he answered for himself, as he was allowed by the Roman laws to do, he pleaded his own cause and showed the falsehood of the charges exhibited against him, observing that as the crimes alleged were reducible to three heads, neither of them were just and true. But Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure, as did his predecessor Felix, he being just entered upon his new government and having met with some caresses and civilities from the Jews at Jerusalem, by whom he had been much pressed and urged about the affair of the apostle. Elsewhere let the slander teach patience. So long as Paul lived under the law his integrity was well known and famous; again, when he was converted to Christ, he was a singular pattern of innocence. Yet we see how he is subject to many slanders, cruel and false accusations; and this is almost always the estate of the servants of Christ, wherefore they must be the more courageous, to pass valiantly through evil report and good report, neither let them think it strange to be evil reported of where they have done good. In the mean season they must do their endeavour that they may not only have a clear conscience before God, but that they may be very well able to defend themselves before men when they have time and place; for Paul doth not fail in his cause, but courageously setteth the defence of his innocency against their false crimes. Furthermore, let us note that the wicked can never be bridled, but they will speak evil of good men, and will impudently slander them, for they resemble the nature of Satan, by whose spirit they are led. Therefore, whereas we be commanded to stop the mouth of the wicked, it must not be so taken as if he who behaveth himself uprightly shall be free from all groundless detraction, but that our life may answer for us, and may wipe away all blots of false infamy. So we see the adversaries of Paul, though they had a favourable judge, yet their slanders were all in vain, seeing he did defend and avouch his innocency by his deeds. On the proposal: whether Festus knew somewhat of their laying await, which we may well conjecture, or whether he were altogether ignorant thereof, he dealeth unjustly with Paul; and we see how soon those are drawn unto all corruption which are not guided by the Spirit of God. For Festus doth not openly contemn or hate Paul, but ambition, and peradventure also desire of gain, got the upper hand, so that, for pleasing the other part, he doth unjustly bring him in danger of death. Notwithstanding, I marvel that he giveth Paul leave to choose, and doth not rather, according to his authority, command them to carry him whether he would or no. Surely we gather that he was kept back with fear, lest he should infringe the privilege of a Roman citizen, which was a very odious crime. Notwithstanding, he studied craftily to persuade Paul not to refuse to be judged at Jerusalem, for he was not ignorant of that which indeed came to pass, that a citizen of Rome might lawfully appeal, so that he could then go no farther. Nevertheless it was no thank to him that he was not delivered into the hands of murderers.

Fix the text, then the charges, then the motive. The strangeness of this mode of expression suggests the thought that our printed text is not quite correct in this place, and this suspicion is confirmed by an examination of manuscripts and versions: not more than eight or ten days is the reading of several of great respectability, with the Coptic, Armenian and Latin. A leading editor admits this reading into the text, and of it a professor of the day says, this is doubtless the genuine reading. The Jews laid many and grievous complaints against Paul: as they must have perceived that the Roman governors would not intermeddle with questions of their law, they no doubt invented some new charges, such as sedition and treason, in order to render the mind of the governor evil affected towards Paul; but their malicious designs were defeated, for assertion would not go for proof before a Roman tribunal. This court required proof, and the blood-thirsty persecutors of the apostle could produce none. While he answered for himself: here only a general account is given, both of the accusations and of the defence; but from the words of this verse the charges appear to have been threefold, that he had broken the law, that he had defiled the temple, and that he dealt in treasonable practices, to all of which he no doubt answered particularly. Willing to do the Jews a pleasure: this was merely to please them and conciliate their esteem, for he knew that, as Paul was a Roman citizen, he could not oblige him to take a new trial at Jerusalem. Elsewhere keep it to a line apiece. Not more than ten days is a short space for a new governor to stay at such a city as Jerusalem; he could not with any convenience have heard and decided the cause of Paul within that time. Bringing many accusations: when many accusations are heaped together, frequently not one of them is true. While he answered: to a general charge a general answer was sufficient. Art thou willing to go up to Jerusalem: Festus could have ordered this without asking Paul, but God secretly overruled the whole, that he might have an occasion of appealing to Rome.

debates: Whether the text reads more than ten days or not more than eight or ten.
What the three counts of the indictment actually were.
Whether the offer of a trial at Jerusalem was a plausible compromise or a betrayal.
Why Festus offered Paul a choice instead of simply ordering him up.
outliers: Clarke reports an editor and a scholar of his day both pronouncing the shorter reading genuine.
Robertson notes the accusers brought no advocate this time and massed their numbers instead.
Ellicott alone defends the fairness of the proposed trial at Jerusalem.
Calvin reasons that fear of violating a citizen’s privilege stayed the governor’s hand.
Wesley observes that heaped-up accusations are usually all false.

10.pericope_label: Then said Paul, I stand at Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest. For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar. Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go

schools.summary: Give the reasons, then the law. The reasons why Paul declined the proposal to be tried at Jerusalem are obvious: he had experienced so much violent persecution from his countrymen, and their minds were so full of prejudice and enmity, that he had neither justice nor favour to hope at their hands. He knew too that they had formerly plotted against his life, and that he had been removed to Caesarea for the purpose of safety; it would be folly to throw himself again into their hands. As he was under no obligation to return, and as Festus did not propose it because justice would be promoted by it but to gratify the Jews, Paul prudently declined and appealed to the Roman emperor. The Roman emperors after the first were all called Caesar, as all the kings of Egypt were called Pharaoh though each had his proper name; the emperor at this time was Nero, one of the most cruel and impious men that ever sat on a throne, and it was under him that Paul was afterwards beheaded. When Paul says he stands at Caesar’s judgment seat he means that he regarded the tribunal before which he then stood, and on which Festus sat, as really the judgment seat of Caesar, for the governor held his commission from the emperor. If I be an offender means, if I have injured the Jews so as to deserve death; and I refuse not to die means, I have no wish to escape justice, nor to evade the laws. No true Christian wishes to escape from the laws: he will honour them, and not seek to evade them; but, like other men, he has rights, and he may and should insist that justice should be done. This bold declaration Paul could make because he knew what the law required, and knew that Festus would not dare to deliver him up contrary to it. Boldness is not incompatible with Christianity, and innocence, when its rights are invaded, is always bold: Jesus firmly asserted his rights when on trial, and no man is under obligation to submit to be trampled on by an unjust tribunal in violation of the laws. On the appeal: by three old statutes it had been enacted that if any magistrate should be about to beat or to put to death any Roman citizen, the accused could appeal to the Roman people, and this appeal carried the cause to Rome; the law was so far changed under the emperors that the cause should be carried before the emperor instead of the people. Every citizen had this right, and when it was made the accused was sent to Rome for trial; a Roman letter-writer of the next generation records that those Christians who were accused and, being Roman citizens, appealed to Caesar, he sent to Rome. The council with which Festus conferred was made up of his associate judges or counsellors in the administration of justice, the chief persons, probably military as well as civil, who were about him. Unto Caesar shalt thou go: he was willing in this way to rid himself of this trial and of the vexation attending it. He did not dare to deliver Paul to the Jews in violation of the Roman laws, and he was not willing to do justice to Paul and thus make himself unpopular with the Jews; he was therefore probably rejoiced at the opportunity of freeing himself from all the trouble in the case, in a manner against which none could object. Elsewhere read the verb and then the constitution. The Greek verb is given in a peculiar form which carries the meaning of, I am standing, and have stood all along. He, as a Roman citizen, claimed the right to be tried by a Roman court, and finding that the procurator had shown a bias which left little hope of a fair trial, exercised the right which attached to his citizenship and appealed to the highest court of all. This interpretation seems every way more rational than that which paraphrases his words thus: I stand already in mind and purpose before the emperor’s court, for God has shown me by a special revelation that I am to preach the gospel at Rome, and my trial there is accordingly part of the divinely ordered course of things which cannot be altered. Whatever influence the earlier promise may have had on the apostle’s conduct, it is scarcely probable that he would have referred to it in this way in giving his reason for appealing. As thou very well knowest is the comparative of the adverb: Festus knew this too well to need any further proof, for he had heard the random charges and had seen the worthlessness of the evidence. No man may deliver me unto them is literally, no man may give me up to them as a favour; the words show that he saw through the simulated fairness of the procurator, and did not shrink from showing that he did so. The history of this right of appeal affords a singular illustration of the manner in which the republic had been transformed into a despotic monarchy. Theoretically the emperor was but the commander-in-chief of the armies of the state, appointed by the senate and acting under its direction; consuls were still elected every year and went through the shadowy functions of their office, and many of the provinces were directly under the control of the senate. But Augustus had contrived to concentrate in himself all the powers that in the days of the republic had checked and balanced the exercise of individual authority: he was supreme pontiff, and as such regulated the religion of the state; permanent censor, and as such could give or recall the privileges of citizenship at his pleasure; and the tribunes’ power, which had originally been conferred so that they might protect members of their order who appealed to them against the injustice of patrician magistrates, was attached to his office. As such he became the final court of appeal from all subordinate tribunals, and so, by a subtle artifice, what had been intended as a safeguard to freedom became the instrument of a centralised tyranny. With this aspect of the matter Paul had of course nothing to do: it was enough for him that by this appeal he delivered himself from the injustice of a weak and temporising judge, and made his long-delayed journey to Rome a matter of moral certainty. There is obviously something like a sneer in the procurator’s acceptance of the decision: he knew, it may be, better than the apostle to what kind of judge the latter was appealing, what long delays there would be before the cause was heard, how little chance there was of a righteous judgment at last. Elsewhere keep to the grammar. I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat is a periphrastic present perfect with the second perfect participle of an intransitive verb: Paul means that he is a Roman citizen before a Roman tribunal. Festus was the representative of Caesar and had no right to hand him over to a Jewish tribunal, and Festus recognised this by saying to Paul, wilt thou. Where I ought to be judged is rather, where I must be judged, for the word expresses necessity; Paul exposes the conduct of Festus with merciless precision. As thou also very well knowest means, as thou also dost understand better than thou art willing to admit, and that this is his meaning is made plain by the confession of Festus to the king later in the chapter. If I am a wrong-doer is a condition of the first class, assuming it to be true for the sake of argument, in the present tense of habit; and have committed anything worthy of death is the same condition with a perfect tense of a single case. I refuse not to die uses an old verb meaning to beg off or decline: I do not beg off dying. But if none of these things is: the verb here means exists, and there is no word for true in the Greek. No man can give me up to them means can legally: Paul is a Roman citizen, and not even Festus can make a free gift of Paul to the council. I appeal unto Caesar is a technical phrase; originally the Roman law allowed an appeal from the magistrate to the people, but the emperor represented the people, and so the appeal to Caesar was the right of every Roman citizen. Paul had crossed his Rubicon on this point. The word for council usually means counsel elsewhere in the New Testament, but here alone an assembly of counsellors; the papyri furnish a number of instances of this sense. Here it apparently means the chief officers and personal retinue of the procurator, his assessors, and these local advisers were a necessity. Some discretion was allowed the governor about granting the appeal: if the prisoner were a well-known robber or pirate it could be refused. Unto Caesar thou shalt go is perhaps a volitive future; one commentator thinks Festus sought to frighten Paul with these words, another suggests they may have been uttered, if not with a sneer, yet with the implication that he little knew what an appeal to Caesar means. But embarrassment will come to Festus: he has refused to acquit this prisoner, and hence he must formulate charges against him to go before Caesar.

Read the privilege, then the liberty it gives us. Because Paul seeth that he is betrayed into the hands of the Jews through the ambition of the governor, he objecteth the privilege of the city of Rome. He had submitted himself modestly if the governor had granted that which was just and equal; now, because the governor doth not his duty willingly, necessity compelleth the holy man to defend himself by law, and by this means the Lord delivereth him again, even when he was almost given over into the hands of the enemies. And whereas he desireth to have his matter handled before Caesar’s judgment seat, he doth not therefore make the doctrine of the gospel subject to the judgment of a profane and wicked man; but being ready to give an account of his faith everywhere, he appealeth from that court where he could no longer hope for equity. Furthermore, though the citizens of Rome did retain their privilege, yet the order was then altered, because the Caesars had taken into their own hands the judging of the people, as if they would be good maintainers and patrons of common liberty. Because those whose consciences do accuse them, and which mistrust their matter, fly unto certain odd excuses and exceptions, Paul turneth away from himself this opinion. And surely the ministers of Christ ought to have no less care to make their innocency known than to save their life. If Paul had flatly denied to answer for himself, the enemies would have triumphed, and the doubtfulness of an evil conscience should have been objected to him to the reproach of the gospel; but now when he citeth the governor himself to be a witness of his integrity, and doth refuse no punishment if he should be found guilty, he cutteth off all occasion of slanderous reports. After that he hath professed that he doth not refuse to die if he be found guilty, he freely useth such helps as he could find at the hands of men. Wherefore, if we be at any time brought into like straits, we must not be superstitious, but we may crave help of the laws and politic order, because it is written that magistrates are made and appointed by God to the praise of the godly. Neither was Paul afraid to go to law under an unbelieving judge, for he which appealeth commenceth a new action. Therefore let us know that God, who hath appointed judgment seats, doth also grant liberty to his to use the same lawfully; therefore those mistake Paul who think that he doth flatly condemn the Corinthians because they require help of the magistrate for defence of their right, seeing he reproveth in that place a manifest fault, to wit, because they could suffer no wrong, and because they were too much set upon suing one another, whereby they caused the gospel to be evil spoken of. On the council: the governors did use to have certain of the chief citizens which did attend upon them, and sat with them in judgment, that they might decree nothing without the consent of the council. Furthermore, it doth seem that Festus pronounced this with indignation when he said interrogatively, Hast thou appealed to Caesar? to wit, because it grieved him that he could not do the Jews such a pleasure as he desired; though I leave that indifferent, because it is neither of any great importance, and it leaneth only to a conjecture. Elsewhere fix the seat and the counsellors. Not that here was a seat in the judgment hall built by Herod for Caesar himself to sit in, should he ever come there, as some have thought; but the seat on which Festus sat is called Caesar’s judgment seat because it was in a Roman court of judicature, and because Festus, who filled it, represented Caesar himself. If I be an offender means against the law of Moses, or the temple at Jerusalem, or Caesar the Roman emperor. When he had conferred with the council means not with the Jewish council, or any part of it that came down on this occasion, but with Roman counsellors, which he had to assist him in judgment when any difficult matters were before him; some versions render it, with his counsellors, and one in the singular, with his counsellor. With these he advised whether it was proper to admit of Paul’s appeal or not, and having had their opinion, he answered.

Attend to the original words. Every procurator represented the person of the emperor in the province over which he presided; and as the seat of government was at Caesarea, and Paul was now before the tribunal on which the emperor’s representative sat, he could say with the strictest propriety that he stood before Caesar’s judgment seat, where, as a freeman of Rome, he should be tried. As thou very well knowest: the record of the trial before Felix was undoubtedly left for the inspection of Festus, for as he left the prisoner to his successor he must also leave the charges against him and the trial which he had undergone; besides, Festus must be assured of his innocence from the trial through which he had just now passed. For if I be an offender: if it can be proved that I have broken the laws so as to expose me to capital punishment, I do not wish to save my life by subterfuges; I am before the only competent tribunal, here my business should be ultimately decided. The words of the apostle are very strong and appropriate. The Jews asked as a favour from Festus that he would send Paul to Jerusalem; Festus, willing to do the Jews this favour, asked Paul if he would go to Jerusalem and there be judged; Paul says, I have done nothing amiss, either against the Jews or against Caesar, therefore no man can make a present of me to them, that is, favour them so far as to put my life into their hands, and thus gratify them by my death. Festus, in his address to the king, admits this and uses the same form of speech: it is not the custom of the Romans gratuitously to give up any one. Much of the beauty of this passage is lost by not attending to the original words. On the appeal: a freeman of Rome who had been tried for a crime and sentence passed on him had a right to appeal to the emperor if he conceived the sentence to be unjust; but even before the sentence was pronounced he had the privilege of an appeal, in criminal cases, if he conceived that the judge was doing any thing contrary to the laws. An appeal to the emperor was highly respected, and the Julian law condemned those magistrates and others having authority, as violaters of the public peace, who had put to death, tortured, scourged, imprisoned or condemned any Roman citizen who had appealed. From the conference with the council we may learn that the appeal of Paul was conditional, else Festus could not have deliberated with his council whether it should be granted, for he had no power to refuse to admit such an appeal. We may therefore understand Paul thus: I now stand before a tribunal where I ought to be judged; if thou refuse to hear and try this cause, rather than go to Jerusalem, I appeal to Caesar. Festus therefore consulted with the council whether he should proceed to try the cause or send Paul to Rome, and it appears that the majority were of opinion that he should be sent. Rather than Hast thou appealed, read, Thou hast appealed unto Caesar, and to Caesar thou shalt go. The Jews were disappointed of their hope, and Festus got his hand creditably drawn out of a business with which he was likely to have been greatly embarrassed. Elsewhere keep it short. All the courts of the Roman governors were held in the name of the emperor and by commission from him. No man can give me up: he expresses it modestly, the meaning is, Thou canst not. I appeal to Caesar, which any Roman citizen might do before sentence was passed. The council: it was customary for a considerable number of persons of distinction to attend the Roman governors, and these constituted a kind of council with whom they frequently advised.

debates: What Paul meant by saying he stands at Caesar’s judgment seat.
Whether the appeal was absolute or conditional on Festus refusing to try the cause.
Whether the governor’s reply was relief, a threat, or a sneer.
Whether a Christian may lawfully invoke the protection of the civil courts.
outliers: Ellicott rejects the reading that Paul was speaking of a divinely revealed journey to Rome.
Clarke traces one Greek word for favour through three speakers in the chapter.
Calvin uses the appeal to defend believers who go to law before unbelieving judges.
Robertson says Paul exposes the governor with merciless precision.
Ellicott turns the right of appeal into a study of the republic’s decline.

13.pericope_label: And after certain days king Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus. And when they had been there many days, Festus declared Paul’s cause unto the king, saying, There is a certain man left in bonds by Felix

schools.summary: Give the history of the two persons. This Agrippa was the son of the Herod of the earlier chapter, and great grandson of Herod the Great. When his father died he was at Rome with the emperor Claudius, who according to the historian was inclined to bestow upon him all his father’s dominions but was dissuaded by his ministers, since it was thought imprudent to bestow so large a kingdom on so young and inexperienced a man; accordingly a procurator was sent to Judea. When Herod the king of Chalcis died, that kingdom was bestowed on Agrippa; afterwards the tetrarchy of Philip and Batanea was added, with Trachonitis and Abila; and after the death of Claudius, Nero added Julius in Perea and a part of Galilee. Agrippa had been brought up at Rome and was strongly attached to the Romans; when the troubles commenced in Judea which ended in the destruction of Jerusalem he did all he could to preserve peace, but in vain, and afterwards joined his troops with those of the Romans and assisted at the destruction of the city. After its captivity he went to Rome with his sister Bernice, where he ended his days at the age of seventy. His manner of living with his sister gave occasion to reports respecting him very little to his advantage. Bernice was his sister, and had been married to Herod king of Chalcis, her own uncle by her father’s side. Festus declared Paul’s case, probably because Agrippa, being a Jew, would be supposed to be interested in it; it was natural that this trial should be a topic of conversation, and perhaps Festus was disposed to ask what was proper to be done in such cases. Left in bonds is in the Greek simply a prisoner: he was left in custody, probably in the keeping of a soldier. Elsewhere make each character a study. Each of the characters thus brought on the scene has a somewhat memorable history. The former closes the line of the Herodian house. He was the son of the Agrippa whose tragic end is related earlier, and was but seventeen at the time of his father’s death; he did not succeed to the kingdom of Judea, which was placed under a procurator, but on the death of his uncle Herod, king of Chalcis, received the sovereignty of that region from Claudius, and with it the superintendence of the Temple and the nomination of the high priests. Four years later he received the tetrarchies that had been governed by his great-uncles Philip and Lysanias, with the title of king, and Nero afterwards increased his kingdom by adding some of the cities of Galilee. He lived to see the destruction of Jerusalem and died at the age of seventy-three. The history of Bernice reads like a horrible romance. She was the eldest daughter of the elder Agrippa, and was married at an early age to her uncle the king of Chalcis; alliances of this nature were common in the Herodian house. On his death she remained for some years a widow, but dark rumours began to spread that her brother, who had succeeded to the principality of Chalcis and who gave her something like queenly honours, was living with her in a yet darker form of incest. On the conversation: the matter seems to have come in, as it were, in the course of talk. Festus probably thought that Agrippa, who knew all about the Jews and their religion, could throw some light on the peculiar position of his prisoner, who, though a Jew and professing the utmost reverence for the Law and the Temple, was yet accused and denounced by his compatriots. Elsewhere keep to the grammar, and let the indignation show. When certain days were passed is a genitive absolute, days intervening. Agrippa the king is the second of the name, son of the Agrippa of the earlier chapter. On the death of Herod king of Chalcis, Claudius gave this Herod Agrippa the throne of Chalcis, so that the historian is correct in calling him king, though he was not king of Judea; he was also given the government of the temple and the right of appointing the high priest, and later the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias. He was the last Jewish king in Palestine. He angered the Jews by building his palace so as to overlook the temple and by frequent changes in the high priesthood, and made his capital at Caesarea Philippi, which he called Neronias in honour of Nero. Bernice was his sister, and yet she lived with him in shameful intimacy in spite of her marriage to her uncle Herod king of Chalcis and to Polemon king of Cilicia, whom she left; one historian calls her both a Jewish bigot and a wanton, and she afterwards became the mistress of Titus. Arrived at Caesarea is a first aorist: they came down to Caesarea from Jerusalem. And saluted Festus should be the aorist middle participle, which cannot mean subsequent action as the revised version gives it, but only contemporaneous action, saluting: the salutation synchronised with the arrival. Tarried is imperfect active, the common verb for spending time, and many days is more days than a few, accusative for extent of time. Laid Paul’s case is a second aorist middle of an old verb meaning to set before or place up, as if for consultation in conference, used only twice in the New Testament. The motive is not given, though it was natural enough in view of the quandary of Festus about Paul and Agrippa’s interest in and responsibility for Jewish worship in the temple; it is quite possible that Festus had a bit of ennui over the visit of these Jewish dignitaries as more days went by. Hence his tone about Paul in this proposal for the entertainment of Agrippa and Bernice is certainly one of superficial and supremely supercilious indifference. Left a prisoner is a perfect passive participle of a verb meaning to leave behind: Paul is one of the leavings of Felix, a sort of junk left on his hands. This cowardly Roman procurator thus pictures the greatest of living men and the greatest preacher of all time to this profligate pair of sinners. Undoubtedly today in certain circles Christ and his preachers are held up to like contempt.

Take the long narration and say what it is for. This long narration tendeth to this end, that we may know that though the handling of the cause were broken off, yet were Paul’s bands famous; and that he was nevertheless brought out of prison, that he might make profession of his faith, and dispute touching the gospel before a famous auditory; and again, that though he were contemned, yet was he not counted a wicked person, lest the glory of Christ should be abased by his slander and reproach; yea, that he had more liberty to preach the gospel being in prison than if he had lived free in a private house. It is certain that this Agrippa was son to Agrippa the elder, whose filthy and detestable death was set down in the twelfth chapter. When this man was made king of Chalcis in his uncle’s stead, after the decease of his father, he did afterward obtain a more large dominion. Bernice, of whom mention is made in this place, was his own natural sister, which was first married to Herod king of Chalcis, her uncle, and did keep herself widow a certain season after his death, yet she did not live honestly and chastely during that time, for her great familiarity with her brother Agrippa was suspected. And to the end she might not be counted an incestuous person, she married with Polemon, king of Cilicia; notwithstanding, because she gave herself more to lust than to chastity, she forsook him. The historiographers do nowhere say that she was her brother’s wife, and one of them assigned her a dominion of her own in part of Galilee. Therefore it is to be thought that, forasmuch as they were hardened in their wickedness, they dwelt together, not regarding what men did say; yet did they abstain from marriage, lest their incestuous marriage should betray and also augment their crime. Neither is it any marvel that he came for honour’s sake to salute the governor. Therefore, when after some time was spent they wanted matter of talk, as idle men use to invent somewhat whereon they may talk, mention was made of Paul; for the historian meant to note that, when he said that after many days were idly spent, Festus told the king of a certain man which lay bound. And although he doth here both touch the malice of the priests and also make a show of wonderful equity on his part, yet in that he shortly after cleareth the party which was accused, he condemneth himself unawares, when he confesseth that he was enforced to appeal that he might not be carried to Jerusalem. But when Festus commendeth the Romans, he showeth what doth beseem judges; and if nature did tell profane men thus much, that they must admit no such favour as may oppress the guiltless, how much more must judges, who have the light of the word of God, be careful to avoid all corruption. Elsewhere mark the idleness. After certain days means several days after the above appeal made by Paul. And when they had been there many days, indulging themselves in pleasure and spending their time in conversing on various subjects, and in order to carry on the conversation and pass away time, the matter of Paul was raised.

Set the scene and read the visit. We have here the preparation that was made for another hearing of Paul before King Agrippa, not in order to his giving judgment upon him, but in order to his giving advice concerning him, or rather only to gratify his curiosity. Christ had said concerning his followers that they should be brought before governors and kings: in the former part of this chapter Paul was brought before Festus the governor, here before Agrippa the king, for a testimony to both. Here is a royal visit. Kings usually think it enough to send their ambassadors to congratulate their friends, but here was a king that came himself, that made the majesty of a prince yield to the satisfaction of a friend; for personal converse is the most pleasant among friends. Observe who the visitants were. King Agrippa was the son of that Herod, surnamed Agrippa, who killed James the apostle and was himself eaten of worms, and great grandson of Herod the Great, under whom Christ was born; the historian calls this Agrippa the younger, and Claudius the emperor made him king of Chalcis and tetrarch of Trachonitis and Abylene. The Jewish writers speak of him, and among other things relate this story: that reading the law publicly in the latter end of the year of release, as was enjoined, the king, when he came to those words, Thou shalt not set a stranger king over thee, who is not of thy brethren, the tears ran down his cheeks, for he was not of the seed of Israel; which the congregation observing, cried out, Be of good comfort, king Agrippa, thou art our brother, for he was of their religion, though not of their blood. Bernice came with him. She was his own sister, now a widow, the widow of his uncle Herod king of Chalcis, after whose death she lived with this brother of hers, who was suspected to be too familiar with her; and after she was a second time married to Polemon king of Cilicia, she got to be divorced from him and returned to her brother. A satirist speaks of a diamond ring which Agrippa gave to Bernice, his incestuous sister, and two historians speak of a criminal intimacy afterwards between her and Titus. Drusilla, the wife of Felix, was another sister. Such lewd people were the great people generally in those times! Say not that the former days were better. What the design of this visit was: they came to salute Festus, to give him joy of his new promotion and to wish him joy in it, to compliment him upon his accession to the government and to keep up a good correspondence with him, that Agrippa, who had the government of Galilee, might act in concert with Festus, who had the government of Judea. But it is probable they came as much to divert themselves as to show respect to him, and to share in the entertainments of his court, and to show their fine clothes, which would do vain people no good if they did not go abroad. Then Festus gave the king an account of Paul, first to entertain him and give him some diversion, for it was a very remarkable story and worth any man’s hearing, and it would be particularly acceptable to Agrippa, not only because he was a judge but much more as he was a Jew; and secondly to have his advice, for Festus was but newly come to be a judge in these parts, and therefore was diffident of his own ability and willing to have the counsel of those that were older and more experienced. He found him a prisoner when he came into the government of this province, and therefore could not of his own knowledge give an account of his cause from the beginning; if there were any thing amiss in the first taking of him into custody, Festus is not to answer for that, for he found him in bonds.

Fill in the two histories from the record. This was the son of the Herod Agrippa of the earlier chapter. Upon the death of his father’s youngest brother Herod, he succeeded him in the kingdom of Chalcis by the favour of the Emperor Claudius; afterwards Claudius removed him from that kingdom to a larger one, giving him the tetrarchy of Philip, which contained Trachonitis, Batanea and Gaulonitis, and likewise the tetrarchy of Lysanias and the province which Varus had governed. Nero made a further addition and gave him four cities: Abila, Julias in Perea, Tarichaea and Tiberias in Galilee. Claudius gave him the power of appointing the high priest among the Jews, and instances of his exercising this power may be seen in the historian. This king was strongly attached to the Romans and did every thing in his power to prevent the Jews from rebelling against them; and when he could not prevail he united his troops to those of Titus and assisted in the siege of Jerusalem, surviving the ruin of his country several years. Bernice, or as she is sometimes called Berenice, was sister of this Agrippa and of the Drusilla mentioned earlier. She was at first married to her uncle Herod king of Chalcis, and on his death went to live with her brother, with whom she was violently suspected to lead an incestuous life; a Roman satirist, as usual, mentions this in the broadest manner, in the verses on the notable diamond made more precious on the finger of Bernice, which a barbarian gave of old to an incestuous woman, and Agrippa gave to his sister. Declared Paul’s cause unto the king: Festus knew that Agrippa was better acquainted with such matters than he was, and he wished in some sort to make him a party in this business. Elsewhere keep it to a sentence. Agrippa was the son of Herod Agrippa, and Bernice his sister, with whom he lived in a scandalous familiarity; this was the person whom Titus so passionately loved that he would have made her empress, had not the clamours of the Romans prevented it.

debates: What brought Agrippa and Bernice to Caesarea, and what the visit was really for.
Whether Bernice was her brother’s wife or only lived with him.
Why Festus raised Paul’s case — idle talk, entertainment, or genuine consultation.
What the phrase left in bonds reveals about the conduct of Felix.
outliers: Henry reports a rabbinic story of Agrippa weeping over the law against a foreign king.
Calvin argues the pair avoided marriage precisely so as not to advertise the incest.
Robertson calls Paul one of the leavings of Felix and the procurator cowardly for saying so.
Calvin holds that Paul had more liberty to preach in prison than he would have had at large.
Henry concludes that one should not say the former days were better.

15.pericope_label: About whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, desiring to have judgment against him. To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him. Therefore, when they were come hither, without any delay on the morrow I sat on the judgment seat, and commanded the man to be brought forth. Against whom when the accusers stood up, they brought none accusation of such things as I supposed

schools.summary: State the Roman rule, and prize it. Festus here states the reasons which he gave to the Jews for not delivering Paul into their hands: the reason of his refusal was that it was contrary to the Roman law. A Roman historian says, it is not their custom to condemn men before they are heard; a Jewish writer says the same thing; and an annalist writes, a defendant is not to be prohibited from adducing all things by which his innocence may be established. It was for this that the equity of the Roman jurisprudence was celebrated throughout the world. We may remark that it is a subject of sincere gratitude to the God of our nation that this privilege is enjoyed in the highest perfection in this land: it is the privilege of every man here to be heard, to know the charges against him, to be confronted with the witnesses, to make his defence, and to be tried by the laws, and not by the passions and caprices of men. In this respect our jurisprudence surpasses all that Rome ever enjoyed, and is not inferior to that of the most favoured nation of the earth. To deliver means to give him up as a favour to popular clamour and caprice; yet our Saviour, in violation of the Roman laws, was thus given up. Have the accusers face to face, that he may know who they are, and hear their accusations and refute them: nothing contributes more to justice than this. Tyrants suffer men to be accused without knowing who the accusers are, and without an opportunity of meeting the charges; it is one great principle of modern jurisprudence that the accused may know the accusers. On the surprise: there was no charge, as Festus expected, of a breach of the peace, of a violation of the Roman law, of atrocious crime. It was natural that he should suppose that they would accuse Paul of some such offence, for Paul had been arraigned before Felix, had been two years in custody, and the Jews were exceedingly violent against him; all this, Festus would presume, must have arisen from some flagrant and open violation of the laws. Elsewhere listen to the tone. The facts of the case are stated with fair accuracy, but there is a certain measure of ostentation in the way in which Festus speaks of the manner of the Romans. It was perhaps natural that a procurator just entering on his term of office should announce, as with a flourish of trumpets, that he at least was going to be rigidly impartial in his administration of justice; and it is fair to state that, as far as we know, his conduct was not inconsistent with his profession. The use of the same verb as that which Paul had used shows that the arrow shot at a venture had hit the mark: Festus is eager to repel the charge. The words to die, literally unto destruction, are not found in the best manuscripts and seem to have been added by way of explanation. The language of the procurator is strictly official: the accused and the accusers are to stand face to face, and the former is to have an opening for his defence in answer to the indictment. Elsewhere keep to the grammar. Informed is the same word used of the earlier plot. Asking for sentence against him uses the only New Testament example of an old word for penalty, fine or condemnation, compounded from the words for against and justice. It is not the custom of the Romans may be direct quotation or indirect discourse after I answered, with the present tense preserved as is usual; there is a touch of disdain in the tone of Festus, and at any rate a tone of scorn towards the Jews. Before that the accused have: this use of the optative in a temporal clause instead of the subjunctive is in conformity with literary Greek and occurs only in this writer in the New Testament, a mark of the literary style occasionally seen in him; it is interesting to note the succession of dependent clauses in these verses. The accusers face to face uses the same word for accuser as earlier. This all sounds fair enough. And have had opportunity to make his defence is literally, and should receive opportunity for defence concerning the charge, the last word occurring in the New Testament only here and once earlier. When they were come together here is a genitive absolute without the pronoun, merely understood; delay is an old word occurring only here in the New Testament. Brought is imperfect active, referring to their repeated charges. Of such evil things as I supposed shows an incorporation of the antecedent into the relative clause and a change of case; note the imperfect to emphasise the state of mind of Festus about Paul before the trial, an old verb occurring only three times in the New Testament.

Weigh the admission, and then the heathen’s blindness. I marvel why Festus doth say that there was no such crime objected to Paul as he supposed, seeing he was accused of sedition; but we may again conjecture by this, yea, plainly know, that their accusations were so vain that they ought not to have been brought before the judgment seat, as if a man did utter a slanderous speech unadvisedly. For which cause he saith that the state of the cause did consist in questions of the law. Therefore we see that he putteth a difference between those offences which were wont to be punished by man’s laws, and the controversy which was between Paul and the Jews; not that religion ought to be violated with impunity, or that their malapertness is tolerable who overthrow the worship of God with their own inventions, but because the man, being a Roman, cared not for Moses’ law. Therefore he speaketh so disdainfully when he saith that they did strive about their superstition, though this Greek word be taken as well in good as in evil part, to wit, because the worshipping of false gods was common in all places. Notwithstanding, his meaning is that he careth not what manner of religion the Jews have. And no marvel if a man which was a heathen, and had not learned that the rule of godliness must be sought from the mouth of God, know not how to distinguish between the pure worship of God and superstitions. Wherefore we must hold fast that mark whereby we may discern the one from the other, that there is no godliness but that which is grounded in the knowledge of faith, lest we grope in darkness. Moreover, the Romans were so drunken with prosperous success that they thought they were more acceptable to God than any other. Elsewhere supply the connections. About whom, when I was at Jerusalem, quickly after he came to his government. To whom I answered, as follows. Therefore when they were come hither, to Caesarea, namely the chief priests and elders of the Jews. Against whom when the accusers stood up, as they were obliged to do whilst they were exhibiting their charges, bearing their testimonies and producing their proofs.

Correct the text, then praise the law. Instead of judgment, condemnation, a sentence of death, is the reading of the best manuscripts, which is probably genuine; and this is evidently the meaning of the place, whichever reading we prefer. Nothing could satisfy these men but the death of the apostle: it was not justice they wanted, but his destruction. It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die means, to make a present of any man, gratuitously to give up the life of any man through favour or caprice. For this righteous procedure the Roman laws were celebrated over the civilized world: a Roman historian says, it is not their custom to condemn men before they have been heard; and a Jewish writer says that, by giving sentence in common and hearing impartially both plaintiff and defendant, not thinking it right to condemn any person unheard, they decided as appeared to them to be just, without either enmity or favour, but according to the merits of the case. England can boast such laws, not only in her statute books but in constant operation in all her courts of justice. Even the king himself, were he so inclined, could not imprison nor punish a man without the regular procedure of the law; and twelve honest men, before whom the evidence has been adduced, the case argued, and the law laid down and explained, are ultimately to judge whether the man be guilty or not guilty. Here, in this favoured country, are no arbitrary imprisonments, no Bastiles, no lettres de cachet. The law makes the king, and the king is the grand executor and guardian of the laws, laws in the eyes of which the character, property and life of every subject are sacred. On the surprise: it was natural for Festus, at the first view of things, to suppose that Paul must be guilty of some very atrocious crime. When he found that he had been twice snatched from the hands of the Jews, that he had been brought to Caesarea as a prisoner two years before, that he had been tried once before the council and once before the governor of the province, that he had now lain two years in bonds, and that the high priest and all the heads of the Jewish nation had united in accusing him and loudly demanded his condemnation, it was natural for him to suppose the apostle to be some flagitious wretch. But when he had tried the case, and heard their accusations and his defence, how surprised was he to find that scarcely any thing that amounted to a crime was laid to his charge, and that nothing that was laid to his charge could be proved. Elsewhere state the rule and the cause of the error. Desiring judgment against him, as upon a previous conviction, which they falsely pretended. It is not the custom of the Romans: how excellent a rule, to condemn no one unheard! A rule which, as it is common to all nations, courts of inquisition only excepted, so it ought to direct our proceedings in all affairs, not only in public but private life. Such things as I supposed: from their passion and vehemence.

debates: Whether the Jews asked for judgment or for a sentence of death.
Whether the governor’s appeal to Roman custom was sincere or ostentatious.
Why the charges fell so far short of what the governor expected.
Whether a heathen magistrate can tell true religion from superstition.
outliers: Barnes and Clarke each turn the Roman rule into a tribute to the courts of their own country.
Ellicott notes that Festus repeats the very word Paul had used about being given up as a favour.
Robertson finds a literary optative here found nowhere else in the New Testament.
Clarke lists the whole record as it would have appeared to an incoming governor.
Calvin infers from the admission that the charges should never have reached a court.

19.pericope_label: But had certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. And because I doubted of such manner of questions, I asked him whether he would go to Jerusalem, and there be judged of these matters. But when Paul had appealed to be reserved unto the hearing of Augustus, I commanded him to be kept till I might send him to Caesar. Then Agrippa said unto Festus, I would also hear the man myself. To morrow, said he, thou shalt hear him

schools.summary: Defend the word, then expose the scorn. Certain questions means certain inquiries, or litigated and disputed subjects, certain points of dispute in which they differed. The word rendered superstition properly denotes the worship or fear of demons, but was applied by the Greeks and Romans to the worship of their gods; it is the same word used earlier at Athens, where it is used in a good sense. There are two reasons for thinking that Festus used it here in a good sense, and not in the sense in which we use the word superstition. First, it was the word by which the worship of the Greeks and Romans, and therefore of Festus himself, was denoted, and he would naturally use it in a similar sense in applying it to the Jews, wishing simply to describe their worship in such language as he was accustomed to use when speaking of religion. Second, he knew that Agrippa was a Jew, and would not probably speak of the religion of his royal guest as superstition, but would speak of it with respect. He meant therefore to say simply that they had certain inquiries about their own religion, but accused Paul of no crime against the Roman laws. Of one Jesus which was dead is in the Greek, of one dead Jesus. It is evident that Festus had no belief that Jesus had been raised up, and in this he would expect that Agrippa would concur with him. Paul had admitted that Jesus had been put to death, but maintained that he had been raised from the dead; as Festus did not believe this, he spoke of it with the utmost contempt: they had a dispute about one dead Jesus, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. In this manner a Roman magistrate could speak of the glorious truth of the Christian religion. Because I doubted of such manner of questions means, because I hesitated about the right way of disposing of them, because I was ignorant of their nature and bearing, I proposed to go to Jerusalem that the matter might be more fully investigated. It is obvious that if Paul was not found guilty of any violation of the laws, he should have been at once discharged; some interpreters understand this as affirming that Festus was not satisfied about the question of Paul’s innocence. To be reserved means to be kept, not to be tried at Jerusalem but to be sent to Rome for trial, that the emperor might hear and decide the cause. The name rendered Augustus properly denotes that which is venerable, or worthy of honour and reverence; it was first applied to the Caesar who was the Roman emperor in the time when our Saviour was born, but the title continued to be used of his successors in office, as denoting the veneration due to the rank of emperor. Agrippa doubtless had heard much of the fame of Jesus and of the new sect of Christians, and probably he was induced by mere curiosity to hear what Paul could say in explanation and defence of the doctrine of Christianity. This wish of Agrippa gave occasion to the noblest defence which was ever made before any tribunal, and to as splendid eloquence as can be found anywhere in any language. Elsewhere trace the words outward. The word rendered superstition is of the same import as that used by Paul at Athens, and the use here shows its comparatively neutral character. Festus was speaking to a Jewish king and would not knowingly have used an offensive term; he falls back accordingly upon one which an outsider might use of any local religion which he did not himself accept.
